prs.title: next-swc: rebuild native when embedded js/src files change
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
## Summary

`pnpm build-all` decides whether to build the native binary with `packages/next-swc/maybe-build-native.mjs`. That script `git diff`s against the last version-bump commit, and only builds when `.rs`, `.toml`, `.cargo/**`, `Cargo.lock` or `rust-toolchain` files changed.

Several crates compile a `js/src` directory into the binary with `embed_directory!`: next-core, turbopack-ecmascript-runtime, turbopack-ecmascript, turbopack-node, turbopack-wasm and turbopack-cli. Editing only those files counted as "no Rust changes", so the script skipped the build. It then deleted the local `native/*.node` in favor of the prebuilt npm binary, so local runtime changes silently never took effect.

This adds `crates/*/js/src/**` and `turbopack/crates/*/js/src/**` to the pathspec.

## Verification

- With only `turbopack-ecmascript-runtime/js/src` files modified, the `git diff --name-only` in `hasRustChanges` now lists them, so the build runs. Before this change it printed nothing.

prs.title: Collect root param dependencies for `'use cache'` at build time
prs.author: unstubbable
prs.body:
`'use cache'` already deduplicates invocations across requests, but joiners must wait for runtime root-param collection before consuming the result. Cache key upgrading preserves isolation at the cost of streaming for those joiners. Root-param redirects also require extra cache-handler writes and lookups for readers without known dependencies.

This change prepares upfront computation of the root-param portion of the cache key. Turbopack collects root param dependencies from generated getter modules and emits them as `rootParamDependencies` in the server-reference manifest. It uses the same traversal helper as env and code-hash collection. Each collector still walks the graph separately.

Cache functions that share a compiled module in the same graph receive the same list of root param dependencies. Conditional and namespace access can also include more root params than an invocation reads. This overkeying is safe but reduces cache reuse. We can improve precision later by giving each cache function its own module.

Imported helpers, re-exports, and resolvable dynamic imports can expose root param dependencies to the collector. Code supplied through runtime values can hide them. For example, a generic cached function can receive a callable reference whose implementation reads a root param outside the cached module's dependency graph.

The `experimental.useCacheStaticRootParamTracking` flag defaults to `false`. Setting it to `true` enables collection in Turbopack production bui
…(truncated)

prs.title: [PPF] Log Sync IO errors in runtime prerenders
prs.author: lubieowoce
prs.body:
Closes NAR-959

Sync IO can deopt the result of a runtime prerender, both in a runtime request and in the embedded runtime prefetch stream.

Long ago, we decided to not log these errors, with the motivation that:
1. The user didn't opt into the runtime prefetch stream
2. They are not reproducible in dev

However:
- 1 is now no longer invalid, because the runtime prefetch stream is only enabled in PPF, which _is_ an opt in.
- 2 is no longer valid, because opening the page in dev reliably reproduces sync IO errors in cacheable content (see [tests](test/e2e/app-dir/instant-validation/sync-io-and-blocking.util.ts#L21))

...so we can now start logging the errors again. This helps the user notice that the deopt is occurring, which they can then go reproduce in dev.

prs.title: Bundle Analyzer Agent Skill: Stream versioned analyzer graph as JSON Lines
prs.author: wbinnssmith
prs.body:
## Summary

Separate analyzer capture from versioned JSON Lines graph replay. `next analyze` builds the analyzer data and serves its UI; `next analyze --output --snapshot-name <name>` saves the usual binary snapshot and UI without serving. `next analyze --export-graph --snapshot-name <name>` reads a saved snapshot and streams one typed JSON record per line **without building or spawning a child**. Bare `--export-graph` reads the newest snapshot; `--snapshot <id>` selects an exact generated ID, and `--route` filters route records. Replay rejects a duplicate/missing name and an explicit `--port`, but accepts inherited `PORT`.

Capture honors the configured `distDir` and holds Next's existing build lock from before Turbopack writes through snapshot completion (or until the UI exits). SWC bindings are installed **before** acquiring that native lock. Replay does not load the app config: apps using a custom directory pass `--dist-dir <relative-dir>` explicitly, leaving stdout as JSON Lines. The authoritative v1 record schema ships with the installed `next` package at `next/analyze/graph-v1.schema.json`; this root layer exports verified base fields, and the stacked producer PRs add typed roots, output membership and load relationships. The former `--output=json` shortcut and `--graph-json` spelling are intentionally rejected. Analyzer-owned filesystem work uses synchronous I/O for capture setup, snapshot persistence/history pruning and graph reads. Export keeps stdout drain handling
…(truncated)

prs.title: Turbopack: Cache canonicalized paths without turbo-tasks, try to find the longest cached prefix first
prs.author: bgw
prs.body:
When converting from an absolute system path to a filesystem-relative path, we'd first try to lexically `strip_prefix`, but if that failed, we'd fall back to trying to canonicalize the root path before stripping.

Because we don't know how many of the path segments refer to the root, we have to canonicalize one path segment at a time.

With turbo-tasks, we have to probe the cache once per path segment, starting from the shortest possible path segment.

This removes the `turbo_tasks::function` we were using to cache the canonicalization calls, and instead stores caches in `BTreeMap`s. This lets us efficiently look up the longest matching prefix in the cache, which (in the happy path) should be a match for a filesystem root.

## Possible concerns

- ~We have duplicated canonicalization caches, one for the map, one for each `DiskFileSystem`. Would a per-process (`OnceLock`) cache of canonicalization calls make more sense?~ We now prefer lookups in the map, which effectively solves this.
- A `PatriciaMap` would likely be more space efficient. `PatriciaMap` is currently only used in `AliasMap`: turbopack/crates/turbopack-core/src/resolve/alias_map.rs#L16

## Things I don't think are concerns

- `RwLock`: If we have a lot of writes, that means we're spending a lot of time doing canonicalization, which would be a bigger problem than locking.

prs.title: turbo-tasks-backend: stop pinning tasks during restores and always discard missing tasks
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
### What?

When `task_pair` or `prepare_tasks` opens a task that is missing from disk (`MustExist`), or a restore hits an I/O error, it panics. They had already pinned the tasks involved (`transient_ref_count += 1`) and never released those pins. Because the missing task was still pinned, its entry also stayed in the map.

Those pins weren't needed, so this removes them instead of making their release more careful:

- `restore_task`, `prepare_tasks` and `task_pair` no longer pin a task while they use its id without holding its lock.
- `handle_missing_task` always discards a missing task's entry. A missing task can't hold a transient reference, because those are only taken on tasks that exist; this is now a debug assertion. A thread still using the id creates a new entry, finds the task missing itself, and discards that entry too.
- `task_pair` discards the entry it created for a missing transient endpoint before panicking.
- `prepare_tasks` keeps handing off every task that does exist and reports missing tasks and I/O errors once at the end.
- `prepare_tasks_with_callback` now documents that its callback must not panic. A panic there is a backend bug, expected to abort. One in Phase 1a can leave this batch's restoring claims set.

### Why?

Previously I considered these panics to be fatal, so being careful about the pins leaking or the entries being discarded wasn't important.  But these panics are sometimes caught by turbo-task functions.  If the failure doesn't propagate th
…(truncated)

prs.title: Keep dev and build running during upgrade prompts
prs.author: devjiwonchoi
prs.body:
Supersedes #99515 and #99516.

> [!TIP]
> Best reviewed commit by commit, hide whitespaces.

### Why?

The upgrade nudge menu blocks `next dev/build` work while it waits for a response. Both should keep running behind the menu, and their output should show up after Skip instead of drawing over it.

### How?

Run the work in a child process whose stdout and stderr are pipes read by the CLI. Everything the child starts (workers, Turbopack, installers) inherits the same pipes, so all output passes through the CLI without touching the code that prints it. `FORCE_COLOR` and the terminal width are passed on because a pipe is not a terminal.

Trade-offs:

- Piped output is not a TTY, so build spinners don't animate. Finished steps and their times are still printed.
- stdout and stderr can be reordered relative to each other.
- An interactive build runs one extra process.
- Turbopack code frames use a fixed width, and SWC errors in webpack use plain ASCII, because native code checks the terminal directly.

Closes NAR-943

prs.title: [turbo-tasks-backend] Clean up task state before publishing execution completion
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
## What?

Task completion now cleans up the task's per-execution state (removing cells that no longer exist, `cleanup_after_execution`) under the same task lock that finishes the execution, before the completion is published (in-progress state removed, `done_event` notified).

Previously the cleanup ran afterwards, under a second lock acquisition. A waiter could invalidate the task in that gap and its next execution could start. The old cleanup would then remove that execution's state, e.g. the `outdated_*_dependencies` it was just given, and could also remove cells it had created.

## Why?

`collectibles_outdated_dependency` fails locally on canary (5/5 runs here) and passes in CI only by timing. Tracing showed the old cleanup observing the next collector execution already running with populated `outdated_collectibles_dependencies`, then clearing them. Later collectible emissions then made the waiting collector stale, so it executed an extra time. The optimization from #99386 assumes that bookkeeping is intact.

There is a second, independent reason the test can see an extra execution: `State::set` invalidates its readers one at a time. The collector can then read the source before the source was invalidated, see the old collectibles, and legitimately re-execute when the new ones arrive.

## How?

- `task_execution_completed_cleanup` now takes the held `TaskGuard`. `task_execution_completed_finish` calls it after setting output and immutability, before dropping the guard and

prs.title: turbo-tasks: bincode-encode copy-on-write snapshots instead of cloning
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
### What?

When a task that is already part of an in-progress persistence snapshot is modified again, `track_modification_internal` now bincode-encodes the task's pre-mutation state into the `SnapshotItem` that persistence will write, and stores that in the `snapshots` map. Before, it stored a `clone_snapshot()` copy of the `TaskStorage`.

### Why?

The copy-on-write path exists so persistence sees a consistent snapshot even if a task is mutated while the snapshot is being written. Cloning `TaskStorage` doesn't guarantee that: cell contents are held behind `SharedReference` (`Arc`), so the clone shares them with the live task. If a cell value has interior mutability, a later mutation shows up in the "frozen" copy and the persisted state is no longer consistent.

Encoding the state right away captures plain bytes that later mutations can't reach. The snapshot iterator hands the stored item straight to persistence, so nothing is encoded twice. The only cost is holding the encoded buffers in memory until the racing persistence picks them up, and this race is rare.

prs.title: [turbo-tasks] Experiment: capture snapshot pending bits under exclusion
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
## Summary

This experiment builds on the copy-on-write snapshot design from #99649, which is now on canary. It holds the operation exclusion while `take_snapshot` runs, so the scan can move modified bits into new `meta_snapshot_pending` / `data_snapshot_pending` bits safely.

Holding the exclusion means a task touched for the first time during the snapshot doesn't need a `None` placeholder in `snapshots`. The map now stores only copy-on-write `SnapshotItem`s, and `end_snapshot` just leaves snapshot mode and clears the map. It no longer has to promote during-snapshot flags or take paired shard locks.

Why: compare this simpler bookkeeping with #99649's approach, which keeps the scan outside the exclusion. The trade-off is that operations stay blocked during the O(N) capture scan. Encoding still happens later in the snapshot iterators, after the exclusion is released. This design was rejected earlier on #99649 ("delaying the snapshot to set these bits is not acceptable"), so this PR is meant for comparison, not as the assumed final direction.

How:
- The scan moves the modified bits into pending bits and records each captured task.
- The first mutation of a captured task encodes all of its pending categories before the mutation, so cases where different categories change in different orders are covered.
- Pending bits stay set until the iterator yields the task. Undo and eviction still see those bits until then.
- Shutdown drain mode still uses the modified bits directly.

prs.title: Update font data and fix no-subsets font fixture
prs.author: wbinnssmith
prs.body:
### What?

Update Google font metadata and generated font declarations, with a coverage-preserving correction to the no-preloadable-subsets fixture.

Related: #99712. This PR includes that font-data update together with the fixture fix; the original PR is left unchanged.

### Why?

Single Day now has a preloadable Latin subset. The existing fixture assumes it has no preloadable subsets and omits subset selection, so default preloading causes font validation to reject it. This repeatedly breaks the webpack development and production font suites.

### How?

Use Noto Sans Math, which still has no preloadable subsets, and update its mocked Google CSS response. Keep preloading implicit so the existing test continues to exercise automatic preload disabling rather than explicit opt-out. Preserve the existing preload-link and attribute assertions without importing source font metadata into the E2E suite.

### Verification

- Webpack development: **22/22 tests passed**.
- Webpack production: **21/21 tests passed**.
- Both modes used React **18.3.1** with experimental strict route types enabled.
- Repository TypeScript check, touched-file ESLint/Prettier checks, and full build passed.
- Local verification used **Node 24**; the CI Node 20 matrix is pending for the latest revision. Both focused suites passed without retries on this revision.

prs.title: Turbopack: report next/font/google font file fetch failures instead of Module not found
prs.author: abhayymishraa
prs.body:
Fixes #97378

### What?

Turbopack turns a failed `next/font/google` font file download into an unresolvable request. Build then dies with:

```
Module not found: Can't resolve '@vercel/turbopack-next/internal/font/google/font'
```

Real cause (`Received response with status 404 when requesting <url>`) shows only as a warning earlier in the log.

### Why?

Hit this on Vercel with 16.3.6 and EB Garamond. Build failed with 56 of these errors, redeploy of same commit passed. Nothing in the error pointed at the font download.

### How?

Font file fetch now follows the stylesheet fetch: error in `next build`, warning in `next dev`. A failed file is served empty, so dev falls back to the next font in the stack. Retries unchanged; `max_retries: 1` already covers connect errors, timeouts and 5xx.

Differs from #97520: dev keeps rendering instead of failing, message comes from the existing fetch issue, and global retry count and webpack mock stay as they are.

### Tests

`test/e2e/next-font/google-font-file-fetch-error.test.ts`, Turbopack only, since webpack in mock mode does not download font files. Mocked stylesheet points at a missing gstatic file.

Without the fix both dev and start fail with `Module not found`. With it both pass. `google-fetch-error` and `index` next-font suites still pass in Turbopack dev and start. `cargo clippy -D warnings`, rustfmt, prettier and eslint clean.
